newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudanese faction sends forces to help army in south.
newsitem.headline: Sudanese faction sends forces to help army in south.

text.p: A southern Sudanese faction is sending its forces to the southern city of Juba to help the Sudanese army fight off an attack, faction leader Riek Machar told Reuters in an interview.
Machar is leader of the South Sudan Independence Movement (SSIM), the largest of five groups which signed a peace agreement with the Khartoum government on Monday.
Machar said he agreed with the government it was the Ugandan army rather than the rebel Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) which was on the offensive in the south.

"The offensive coming from the south is not an SPLA offensive, it is the Ugandan army invading the Sudan. We have a right to defend the peace agreement and Sudanese territory," he said in the interview on Wednesday evening.

"Yes, we have moved troops and are still moving troops to Juba to defend it and even push back the foreign invasion," the SSIM leader added. Earlier this month Machar moved 3,000 of his troops to Juba to help the army.

The mainstream SPLA, the southern group with the largest military force, has rejected the peace agreement, saying it wants to overthrow the Islamist government in Khartoum. It is fighting in alliance with northern opposition forces under the umbrella of the National Democratic Alliance (NDA).
SPLA forces have captured the town of Yei, 130 km (80 miles) southwest of Juba. Their northern allies have launched a separate offensive in northeast Sudan, near the Eritrean border.
Machar defended the peace agreement as a solution to the long war in the south and said SPLA leader John Garang was rejecting it only out of deference to his northern allies.
"The south problem is resolved finally. The south has for a long time wanted to exercise the right to self-determination. This has been granted," he said.
The peace agreement calls for a referendum among southern Sudanese after an interim period of four years to find out whether they want to secede or remain part of Sudan.
"The south is going to have an army, a government and will exercise the right to self-determination in an internationally monitored referendum and will be democratic," Machar said.
Opponents of the agreement say the Islamists who dominate the Khartoum government can use the interim period to change the demographic status quo in the south.

"Unless Garang dissociates himself from the northern opposition, which is only bidding for power, we don't believe he is fighting for the southern Sudan," Machar said. The faction leader said Garang would have trouble persuading his forces to keep fighting.
